title: Mass-Energy Equivalence Relation
short_intro: Mass-energy equivalence establishes that mass and energy are manifestations of the same underlying physical entity, connected by the square of the speed of light in a vacuum. It forms a foundational pillar of special relativity and governs both nuclear transformations and relativistic dynamics.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Understanding the formula E = mc² and its application in basic mass defect and binding energy calculations for atomic nuclei.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Derivation of the relativistic mass-energy relation using momentum and velocity transformations, total energy, kinetic energy, and the relativistic energy-momentum invariant relation.

prerequisites: Conservation of linear momentum and energy in collisions
Lorentz transformation and relativistic mass variation

concept_notes.heading: Inertial Mass and Rest Energy
bullets: Every object of rest mass m<sub>0</sub> possesses an intrinsic rest energy given by E<sub>0</sub> = m<sub>0</sub>c².
Mass is not conserved independently in nuclear and subatomic reactions; rather, the total relativistic energy is conserved.
The rest energy represents the internal energy content of a system when it is stationary in a given inertial frame.

concept_notes.heading: Relativistic Total Energy and Kinetic Energy
bullets: The total relativistic energy of a particle moving with velocity v is E = gamma m<sub>0</sub>c², where gamma = (1 - v²/c²)<sup>-1/2</sup> is the Lorentz factor.
Relativistic kinetic energy K is defined as the difference between total energy and rest energy: K = E - E<sub>0</sub> = (gamma - 1)m<sub>0</sub>c².
In the limit v << c, the relativistic kinetic energy reduces to the classical expression (1/2)m<sub>0</sub>v² via binomial expansion.

concept_notes.heading: Energy-Momentum Invariant Relation
bullets: The total energy E and relativistic momentum p of a particle satisfy the invariant relation E² = p²c² + (m<sub>0</sub>c²)².
For massless particles such as photons, m<sub>0</sub> = 0, which leads directly to the relation E = pc.
The quantity E² - p²c² is invariant under Lorentz transformations for all observers in inertial frames.

concept_notes.heading: Mass Defect and Nuclear Binding Energy
bullets: The mass of an atomic nucleus is always less than the sum of the masses of its constituent free nucleons (protons and neutrons).
The mass difference Delta m, known as mass defect, is equivalent to the total binding energy B of the nucleus released during formation: B = Delta mc².
Positive binding energy signifies a stable bound system, requiring external energy input to separate the nucleons.

derivations.title: Derivation of Relativistic Kinetic Energy and Mass-Energy Equivalence
derivations.conditions: A particle of rest mass m<sub>0</sub> accelerated by a force F along a straight line in an inertial frame.
steps: Start with the work-energy theorem: Work done W = int F dx = Delta K, where F = dp/dt = d(mv)/dt.
Substitute force into the work integral: K = int v d(mv) = int v d(gamma m<sub>0</sub> v).
Expand the differential using the product rule: d(gamma m<sub>0</sub> v) = m<sub>0</sub> v dgamma + gamma m<sub>0</sub> dv.
Substitute gamma = (1 - v²/c²)<sup>-1/2</sup> to find v dgamma = gamma^3 (v^3/c^2) dv and integrate to obtain K = (gamma - 1)m<sub>0</sub>c².
Define total energy E as K + m<sub>0</sub>c², yielding E = gamma m<sub>0</sub>c² = mc².

derivations.title: Derivation of the Energy-Momentum Invariant Relation
derivations.conditions: Relativistic particle with rest mass m<sub>0</sub>, total energy E, and momentum p.
steps: Write the expression for total energy: E = gamma m<sub>0</sub>c².
Write the expression for relativistic momentum: p = gamma m<sub>0</sub>v.
Square both quantities: E² = gamma^2 m_0^2 c^4 and p²c² = gamma^2 m_0^2 v^2 c^2.
Subtract p²c² from E²: E² - p²c² = gamma^2 m_0^2 c^4 (1 - v^2/c^2).
Use the definition gamma^2 = (1 - v²/c²)<sup>-1</sup> to simplify the right-hand side to (m<sub>0</sub>c²)².

graphs_and_experiments.title: Kinetic Energy vs Velocity (Classical vs Relativistic)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of kinetic energy on the y-axis against velocity v/c on the x-axis ranging from 0 to 1. Show two curves: a parabolic curve for classical kinetic energy (1/2)m_0v^2 and an asymptotic curve shooting to infinity at v = c for the relativistic kinetic energy.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: At low speeds (v << c), classical and relativistic kinetic energies coincide. As v approaches c, the relativistic kinetic energy diverges, demonstrating that infinite energy is required to accelerate a massive particle to the speed of light.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually in multiple-choice questions regarding the failure of classical mechanics at high velocities.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Binding Energy Per Nucleon vs Mass Number Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve plotting B/A (Binding energy per nucleon) on the y-axis against mass number A on the x-axis, peaking around A = 50 to 60 (Iron group) with a value of ~8.8 MeV/nucleon, and sloping downwards for light and heavy nuclei.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The peak at intermediate mass numbers explains why nuclear fusion of light nuclei and nuclear fission of heavy nuclei both result in an increase in binding energy per nucleon, releasing mass energy in the process.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently used in PGT and TGT questions to analyze stability, fission, and fusion reactions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Cockcroft-Walton Proton-Lithium Particle Accelerator Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic diagram of a proton beam striking a lithium target resulting in two alpha particles, with a corresponding energy balance equation showing mass converted to kinetic energy.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Direct experimental verification of E = mc² where the kinetic energy of the resulting alpha particles exceeds the kinetic energy of the incident proton by exactly the mass-energy equivalent of the mass defect of the nuclear reaction.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Cited in descriptive questions or numerical problems regarding quantitative verification of mass-energy equivalence in nuclear reactions.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the energy released in joules when 1 microgram (1 mu g) of mass is completely converted into energy.
solution_steps: Identify given values: mass m = 1 mu g = 1 \times 10^{-9} kg, speed of light c = 3 \times 10^8 m/s.
Apply the mass-energy equivalence formula: E = mc^2.
Substitute the values: E = (1 \times 10^{-9} \text{ kg}) \times (3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s})^2.
Calculate the final product: E = 1 \times 10^{-9} \times 9 \times 10^{16} = 9 \times 10^7 \text{ J}.

solved_numericals.question: Find the momentum of an electron whose kinetic energy is equal to its rest mass energy.
solution_steps: Given condition: Kinetic energy K = m_0 c^2.
Total energy E = K + m_0 c^2 = m_0 c^2 + m_0 c^2 = 2 m_0 c^2.
Use the energy-momentum relation: E^2 = p^2 c^2 + (m_0 c^2)^2.
Substitute E: (2 m_0 c^2)^2 = p^2 c^2 + (m_0 c^2)^2.
Expand and rearrange for momentum: 4 (m_0 c^2)^2 - (m_0 c^2)^2 = p^2 c^2 implies 3 (m_0 c^2)^2 = p^2 c^2.
Solve for p: p = \frac{\sqrt{3} m_0 c^2}{c} = \sqrt{3} m_0 c.

solved_numericals.question: A particle of rest mass m_0 moves with a velocity v = 0.8c. Calculate its total relativistic energy and its relativistic momentum in terms of m_0 and c.
solution_steps: Calculate total energy E = \gamma m_0 c^2 = \frac{5}{3} m_0 c^2.
Calculate relativistic momentum p = \gamma m_0 v = \frac{5}{3} m_0 (0.8 c) = \frac{5}{3} \cdot \frac{4}{5} m_0 c = \frac{4}{3} m_0 c.
solved_numericals.answer: E = \frac{5}{3} m_0 c^2 \text{ and } p = \frac{4}{3} m_0 c

assumptions_and_limitations: The relation E = mc² applies strictly in inertial reference frames.
In non-inertial frames, pseudo-forces must be accounted for, modifying the simple form of relativistic energy equations.
The speed of light c is assumed to be an absolute universal constant in all inertial frames as per Einstein's second postulate.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Mass and energy are two completely different physical quantities that happen to be proportional.
common_misconceptions.correct: Mass and energy are two different measures of the exact same physical property of a system.
common_misconceptions.why: E = mc² implies that energy has mass and mass has energy; they are interchangeable manifestations.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The formula E = mc² can be used for any object regardless of whether it is at rest or in motion.
common_misconceptions.correct: E = mc² strictly represents rest energy when m is rest mass, or total energy when m is relativistic mass.
common_misconceptions.why: For a moving particle, the complete energy equation is E = \gamma m_0 c^2 or E^2 = p^2 c^2 + (m_0 c^2)^2.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A massive particle can reach the speed of light if given infinite kinetic energy.
common_misconceptions.correct: A massive particle cannot reach or exceed the speed of light.
common_misconceptions.why: As velocity approaches c, the Lorentz factor and required kinetic energy approach infinity.

quick_revision: Rest energy is given by E_0 = m_0 c^2, and total relativistic energy is E = \gamma m_0 c^2.
Relativistic kinetic energy is K = ( \gamma - 1 ) m_0 c^2.
The fundamental energy-momentum invariant is E^2 - p^2 c^2 = (m_0 c^2)^2.
Mass defect in nuclei directly accounts for the nuclear binding energy via B = \Delta m c^2.
